extracted.intended_audience: nonprofit organizations and grant writers seeking funding (community-based groups, small agencies, program directors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing, targeting, and writing grant proposals for nonprofit organizations, including planning, locating funders, approaching funders, submission logistics, and drafting each proposal section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility and resource assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Can our organization carry it out? Do we have the resources to do it? Could we get the resources we would need? What resources are available?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask detailed questions about internal capacity and available resources before proposing the strategy; consider whether additional resources are obtainable and what currently exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify potential blockers and mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Who or what might prevent us from carrying out the proposal? Why would they try to prevent us from carrying out the proposal? Could we alter the strategy to eliminate these 'blockers'? Would altering the strategy seriously affect the outcome we want?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate opposition and design adjustments to remove barriers without undermining objectives; evaluate the trade-offs of altering strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client participation and uptake
rubrics_metrics.description: Would our clients take advantage of the program or use it as we hope they will? Would our clients even participate? What would ensure their participation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess demand and design features or incentives to ensure intended beneficiaries will engage with the program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess negative side effects and affected parties
rubrics_metrics.description: What other ill effects might this strategy have? Who could be affected?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider unintended consequences and identify stakeholders who might be harmed or adversely affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research and information needs
rubrics_metrics.description: What could help us find out more about this kind of strategy?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify data, pilot tests, expert consultations, or literature needed to strengthen the proposal and reduce uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-effectiveness and alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Is this the easiest or cheapest way to solve the problem? What would be easier or cheaper? Where could we cut corners?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare alternative strategies for feasibility, cost, and impact; be explicit about why chosen strategy is preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justifiability of investment (cost vs results)
rubrics_metrics.description: Will the investment which this solution requires be justifiable in terms of the results expected?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh expected outcomes against costs; show that requested funds are reasonable relative to projected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of prior attempts and outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Has another organization tried this approach? Were they successful? Has this been tried by businesses? Other countries? Were they successful?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document prior implementations, outcomes, and lessons learned to demonstrate feasibility and likelihood of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with organizational philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Is this kind of strategy consistent with our organization's philosophy?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure proposed work aligns with mission, values, and strategic priorities; funders look for mission-fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staff buy-in and comfort
rubrics_metrics.description: Would staff feel at ease working this strategy?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess staff readiness, training needs, and morale implications; include staff capacity notes in the proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid duplication of existing services
rubrics_metrics.description: Does this strategy duplicate other services?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map existing local services to demonstrate uniqueness or collaboration and to avoid redundancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with funder forms, certifications, and deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: If special forms or certification are required, this should be determined in advance. Determination of deadlines is extremely important because many grants are awarded only once a year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify required certifications/forms early, confirm deadlines (postmark vs receipt), and plan timeline accordingly; missing forms can cause immediate rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain local support and stakeholder sign-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be necessary for various local organizations and others who may be affected by the proposed program to agree with the project. Discussions should be initiated with these groups and individuals to explain the project and solicit their support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear proposal with board members, project collaborators, clients, support agencies, and federal regional agency if applicable; secure genuine letters of support addressed to agency director or board chairman that reflect knowledge of the organization and project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local publicity and community relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective local publicity campaigns are often overlooked in planning a proposal. Articles in local newspapers as well as information releases to important persons will help generate support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use local media and outreach to prevent misunderstanding/opposition; reviewers may contact community references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity and format of support letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Only those letters that are addressed to the agency director or board chairman and clearly reflect knowledge of the proposing organization, its work and track record, familiarity with proposed project, and pledge of assistance to the organization, should be included in a proposal package.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague or obviously solicited endorsements; include only substantive, personalized endorsements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for continuation and sustainability
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration should be given to the problem of continuing the project or service after the initial grant runs its course, usually one to three years. What alternative sources of funding might pick up the program?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address long-term funding, scaling, and succession in the proposal's Future Orientation; identify potential follow-on funders or revenue sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of expert advice and technical assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Getting expert advice also can be very helpful in refining your ideas and in bringing credibility to your project. Utilize the services of professionals whenever possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite consultants, fund-raising experts, state technical assistance staff, local professionals, and educational institutions; list relevant resource centers (Foundation Center, Donors Forum, Grantsmanship Center, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Locate appropriate funding sources (do your homework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations must do their homework to know which public and private sector funders to approach for specific projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research foundations, corporations, government programs, and the types of support they offer (grants, loans, matching funds, seed capital); use library and Foundation Center resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approaching government agencies — NOFA and program research
rubrics_metrics.description: On the federal level, organizations can find out about grant programs and their application procedures by reviewing the Federal Register which publishes federal agencies' Notices of Fund Availability (NOFAs). The NOFA will provide information on an application's due date, information contact, legislation, program objectives, allocation and distribution of funds, eligibility, application process and selection criteria for award of funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the NOFA carefully to match eligibility, objectives, deadlines, and selection criteria; note whether unsolicited proposals are accepted and whether discretionary set-asides exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government approach checklist (program status, eligibility, pre-application, decision-makers, decision factors, application process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research program status, eligibility requirements, whether pre-applications are available, who decides awards, and the factors involved in selecting successful applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find appropriation levels, application cycles, responsible office/unit, willingness of agency staff to advise, and historical award patterns to tailor the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approaching corporations and foundations — know the funder
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn as much as possible about the corporation or foundation: past support, objectives, board relationships, geographical interest, grant application information, and financial data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor requests to funder's interests (be specific, selective), approach local management first, state whether funding is for general operating or special project support, and include appropriate enclosures (case statement, audit, board list, 501(c)(3), proposed budget, brochures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brief and targeted proposal letters for some funders
rubrics_metrics.description: Some funding sources do not require proposals but proposal letters instead. The letter request should not be more than two pages in length. Organizations should be able to sell themselves in the first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep letters concise, state the need and request early, follow up with phone call and appointment, research the proper contact name (avoid 'Dear Friend').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid common grantseeking errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Common errors include: lack of knowledge of the donor; sending proposals intended for governmental review to private/corporate funders; making unrealistic demands; expensive packaging; invitations to benefit affairs; mass distribution of the same proposal; failure to follow up; failure to use your Board of Directors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research funders, tailor proposals to funder type, be realistic about amounts and duration, focus on content over expensive packaging, use board relationships, and follow up on contacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission logistics and adherence to funder procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether stated deadlines are postmarked deadlines or receipt deadlines. Send originally signed proposals by overnight mail if necessary, requesting a signed receipt. Remember that some grant programs require the submission of as many as ten copies while others may require only one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow submission instructions exactly, allow time for required state clearinghouse sign-offs, track number of copies, signatures, and delivery receipts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting the proper funding agency — match priorities and capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider current priorities and interests of funding agencies, total funds available, size of a typical grant, nature of a typical grant, percentage of proposals approved, limitations specified in guidelines, matching funds required, and payment and budgeting procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target funders whose priorities, grant size range, and funding mechanisms match your project; determine match requirements (cash vs in-kind) and payment terms (cost reimbursement vs advance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing considerations for proposal submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider congressional or general assembly appropriation schedules, foundation schedules for board meetings, accelerated federal agency action at the end of the fiscal year, and local government budgeting dates if local funds are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan submission calendar around funder decision timelines and potential external accelerations to improve chances of funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate contacts and decision-makers
rubrics_metrics.description: It is helpful to know who will be judging your work. Cultivate a personal contact with the staff person assigned to review projects in your area of interest, if possible. Be prepared to make your case immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop relationships with reviewers/staff, be professional and appreciative (send thank you notes), and be prepared to present a concise case when contacted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track contacts and follow-up activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a chart to track all contacts, both written and verbal, made with various funders. Included items: funding source name, contact person, letters of inquiry, acceptance/rejection, thank you notes, proposal submitted, backup documents submitted, grant interview, on-site visit, date of decision, amount requested, amount granted, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a detailed contact and follow-up log to avoid oversights and to manage multiple funder approaches (recommended to line up four prospects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal writing style and proofreading rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Use simple language, jargon free; avoid using the same words too often; proofread for typographical, grammatical errors, and misspellings; read the proposal out loud; have staff and external readers check for clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt clear, plain language; perform multiple proofreading passes; solicit outside readers for clarity and persuasiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget verification and required attachments
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify budget numbers, cross check and double check for accuracy; be sure to attach a copy of the organization's 501(c)(3), board listing, last audit report, resumes, annual report, brochures, letters of support, and any press releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure financials are accurate and supported with organizational documentation; include all listed enclosures to strengthen credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and physical presentation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Never use script type, keep paragraphs to six lines or less, use larger print type such as pica, not elite; do not use spiral binders; make sure all pages and attachments are numbered and clearly labeled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reader-friendly typography and pagination; avoid fancy or hard-to-handle binding; label appendices clearly for reviewer convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include ten key components in every grant proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: Every grant proposal should include ten key components (given in sequence): Cover Letter, Title Page, Summary, Introduction, Problem Statement, Objectives, Methodology, Evaluation, Future Orientation, Budget, Appendix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow a consistent structure to ensure reviewers find required information; include appendices with supporting documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover Letter requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: On organization letterhead, the cover letter briefly summarizes need, the proposed program, the organization's qualifications and a small sales pitch. The cover letter tells the funding agency who you are and what you do, preferably in 25 words or less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the problem, solution/method, total project cost and requested amount, demonstrate enthusiasm, and have the board chairman sign (executive director may sign 'for the Board' with declaration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Title Page contents
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes project title, name of applicant, name of agency submitted to, signature, typed name and title of authorized personnel approving submission and date of approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear administrative metadata so reviewers know who and what is being submitted and that submission is authorized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary (abstract) guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Synopsis of project objectives, procedures, evaluation. Try to catch the 'flavor' of the project in approximately 250 words. Identifies the applicant organization and establishes its credibility; states the need or problem; outlines objectives, specific activities, total project cost, percentage already committed, and amount asked for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the summary last, be specific, simple, and clear; remember this may be the only part reviewers read in the body of the proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction (organization description)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tells what needs to be done and why. Show your organization's background, qualifications, capability in addressing the stated problem and why you are unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight staff, board, affiliations, clients, volunteers, facilities, past performance, fiscal responsibility, prior funding, and the demonstrated need—without excessive organizational history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem Statement requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: State why this problem needs to be addressed and provide references to research, statistics, previous projects or other documentation which supports the need for the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the constituency's need (not the agency's), use local data (national only for comparison), avoid exaggeration, include research and links to other experts/programs, and present a single, optimal solution rather than multiple options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectives — measurable and client-focused
rubrics_metrics.description: State the proposed outcome of the project in clearly specified and measurable terms. Objectives should be described in terms that are measurable and quantifiable and stated using the client’s point of view and deal with a terminal nature - what the clients will look like at the project's conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each objective links to needs, methodology, and evaluation. Consider objectives as input, process, or impact types; remember the five essential parts for writing objectives (start with 'What').

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology — activities and rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the problem in terms of the methods you will use in combating it and why you are choosing this strategy. Specific activities and action steps used to achieve the objectives should be described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a clear, stepwise plan linking activities to objectives and demonstrating why chosen methods will produce intended outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation — measurement and dissemination
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide details on how the organization and the funding source will determine whether the project has accomplished its objectives. Include the type of evaluation information to be collected, how it will be analyzed and a pattern for its dissemination and use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strengthen this section with specific evaluation criteria tied to each objective, data collection methods, analysis plans, timelines, and reporting procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future Orientation / sustainability planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss all topics relevant to the future of the project, whether its timeframe is limited or if the intent is to continue or expand the project beyond the project time period. How will continuation be done - what future funding has been lined up?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address scalability, continuation funding, institutionalization, and how outcomes will be sustained after grant period ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget — complete and documented costs
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement of the proposed project in terms of costs. Every item should be carefully documented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide detailed, accurate line-item budgets, justify costs, indicate committed funds, and align budget with methodology and objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendix / supporting documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of all required support documentation deemed necessary by the funding source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attach 501(c)(3), audit reports, board lists, resumes, letters of support, brochures, press releases, and any other requested backup materials; number and label appendices clearly.
